stem: Which of the following best explains why consumer spending rose in the 1950s?

options.text: Families spent wartime savings and credit on cars, homes, and appliances
A renewed rush to buy stocks drove most household spending
options.misconception: Background from the books: families bought cars, homes, and appliances, not stocks; stock speculation did not drive the consumer boom.

options.text: The government banned advertising so families saved instead of spending
options.misconception: Background from the books: advertising boomed in the 1950s and stoked demand; the government never banned it.

options.text: Wartime rationing continued and forced families to keep buying
options.misconception: Background from the books: rationing ended with the war; spending rose because goods were available again.

rationales.A: Background from the books: workers had earned money during the war but found few goods to buy, so they spent freely once factories returned to civilian goods.
rationales.B: Background from the books: families bought cars, homes, and appliances, not stocks; stock speculation did not drive the consumer boom.
rationales.C: Background from the books: advertising boomed in the 1950s and stoked demand; the government never banned it.
rationales.D: Background from the books: rationing ended with the war, and spending rose because civilian goods were available again.
rationales.general:
1. Ask where the spending money came from and what it bought.
2. Background from the books: wartime workers earned money with few goods to buy, and credit cards spread after the war to make buying easy.
3. Cars, homes, and appliances were the purchases, not stocks, and rationing was over.
Remember: A spending boom needs money saved, goods to buy, and a way to pay.
